2.text: like living men, and at the end of the story they are petrified.¹ In various

3.text: parts of the territory of the Koryak, mountains, mainly detached cliffs on

4.text: steep rocky capes, usually called “grandfather” (epeˊpil, apaˊpêl²), are pointed

5.text: out. These are often considered as the ancestors of the tribe, mostly Big-

7.text: The same belief exists also among the Kamchadal, who point out among

8.text: the mountains their petrified ancestor Kutq, together with his house, his

9.text: sledge, his hammer, etc. The Kamchadal in former times brought sacrifices

10.text: to all these stones, as do the Koryak now.

11.text: Among the Chukchee the belief is less apparent. However, one cliff on

12.text: the middle of the Anadyr River is called Peruˊten, which is one of the

13.text: names of the sea-god Kereˊtkun. It is told that the latter, when ascending

14.text: the Anadyr River, was so tired that he sat down to rest, and turned to

15.text: stone. Cliffs with the name Epeˊpil are also found in the territory of the

16.text: Chukchee. One, for instance, is situated in the north of Anadyr, not far

17.text: from Mariinsky Post. I am not sure, however, that this idea is free from

18.text: foreign influence. Even the word “epeˊpil” is rather Koryak than Chukchee.

19.text: In Koryak it signifies “little father,” “grandfather:” in Chukchee it belongs

20.text: to the trading-jargon, and signifies the Russian “priest.”³

21.text: In the last stage (the fifth) the personified vital force become completely

22.text: separated from the material objects, and independent of them. There is

23.text: developed a conception of supernatural beings who fill the whole exterior

24.text: world, and move freely within its limits. These beings are anthropomorphous,

25.text: but more powerful than men; they are invisible, but may appear at will to

26.text: various persons, or are seen by shamans even, against their own will.

27.text: ¹ See Bogoras, American Anthropologist, Vol. IV, p. 643; Jochelson, Yukaghir Materials, p. 101. Stories about

28.text: the mountains, quite similar to those of the Yukaghir, were in vogue among the Aleut. Thus, according to a

29.text: native story in Veniaminoff (cited from Elie Reclus, Les Primitifs, p. 59), the mountains on Unimak and

30.text: Unalashka once wrestled, and threw fire and stones at one another. Several smaller volcanoes, who could not

31.text: fight against the larger ones, split, and were extinguished. Only two large mountains were left, Makushin and

32.text: Retcheshnoy. Stones, fire, and ashes killed every living thing. Retcheshnoy was vanquished, and, when he

33.text: saw his defeat, he mustered his remaining force, and swelled himself to the utmost. Then he burst and was

34.text: extinguished. Makushin went to sleep, and now only a light smoke sometimes issues from him. This tale is

35.text: quite similar to that told by Jochelson.
